## Why Reproducible Reporting?

Every report you've made so far this semester has lived in a notebook or
script, with results you'd have to manually copy into an email or a
slide if someone else needed to see them. That copy-paste step is exactly
where real mistakes happen: a chart gets pasted from last week's run, a
number gets fat-fingered, a Word doc goes stale the moment the underlying
data changes.

A **Quarto document** solves this by combining three things in one file:
**narrative text** (like this paragraph), **live code** (that actually
runs), and the **results of that code** (numbers, tables, charts) --
woven directly into the finished report. Change the data, click Render
again, and every number and chart updates itself. Nothing to copy, and
nothing to go stale.

## Anatomy of a Quarto Document

Three pieces, all visible in this very file:

1. **The YAML header** -- the `---` block at the very top of this file,
   with `title:` and `format:`. This is metadata about the whole
   document: what to call it, and what kind of file to produce when
   rendered (`html`, `pdf`, or `docx` are the common choices).
2. **Markdown text** -- ordinary prose, like this bullet list, written in
   the same Markdown syntax you've seen in Jupyter notebooks all
   semester (`##` for a heading, `**bold**`, `-` for a bullet).
3. **Code chunks** -- a block of real, running R code, marked off by
   three backticks and curly braces: ` ```{r} ` to start, ` ``` ` to end.
   Everything between those markers actually executes when you render.

Here is a real code chunk, loading the dataset used throughout this file:

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
sales <- read_csv("retail_sales_clean.csv")
```

Notice nothing printed above except the code itself -- that's the
`#| message: false` **chunk option** on the first line, which tells
Quarto to run this code but hide the routine "columns loaded" message
`read_csv()` normally prints. Chunk options always start with `#|` and go
at the top of a chunk, before any real code.

## Inline Code -- Weaving a Computed Value into a Sentence

This is the single most useful trick in reproducible reporting: putting a
small piece of R code directly inside a sentence, so the *number itself*
updates automatically every time you re-render.

This dataset contains `r nrow(sales)` rows. The highest-revenue store is
`r sales |> group_by(store) |> summarise(total = sum(revenue)) |> arrange(desc(total)) |> slice(1) |> pull(store)`.

Look at the raw text of this file (not the rendered output) to see how
that works: a single backtick, the letter `r`, a space, then a short
piece of R code, then a closing backtick -- all sitting right inside a
normal sentence. When rendered, each one is replaced by whatever that
code actually evaluates to. Change the data, re-render, and both numbers
update themselves -- no manual editing, and no risk of the text and the
number disagreeing with each other.

## A Full Example: Combining Classes 19–21 Into One Report

This section ties together everything from the last three classes --
loading data, cleaning, `dplyr` analysis, and a `ggplot2` chart -- into
one flowing narrative, exactly the way a real report would present them.

### Revenue by Category

```{r}
#| label: fig-category-revenue
#| fig-cap: "Total revenue by category"
category_totals <- sales |> group_by(category) |> summarise(total_revenue = sum(revenue))

ggplot(category_totals, aes(x = category, y = total_revenue)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Total Revenue by Category", x = "Category", y = "Total Revenue ($)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

As @fig-category-revenue shows, electronics generates by far the most
revenue of any category -- more than double the next closest category.
This single chunk does everything: computes the summary with `dplyr`
(Class 20), builds the chart with `ggplot2` (Class 21), and embeds the
finished image directly into this report, all from one source file.

Note the `#| label:` and `#| fig-cap:` chunk options above -- `label`
gives the chunk (and its figure) a name Quarto can cross-reference, and
`fig-cap` sets the caption shown under the chart. The `@fig-category-revenue`
reference in the text above the chunk automatically turns into "Figure 1"
(or whichever number is correct) when rendered -- another thing you never
have to update by hand if a chart's position in the report changes later.

### Controlling What Shows Up: More Chunk Options

```{r}
#| echo: false
top_category <- category_totals |> arrange(desc(total_revenue)) |> slice(1)
```

The chunk above computed something (`top_category`), but **you never saw
the code for it** in the rendered output -- only its result will show up
if we reference it inline. That's `#| echo: false`: it means "run this
code, but don't show the code itself in the final report." This is the
normal choice for a report meant for a non-technical reader, who cares
about the finding (electronics leads with
$`r format(round(top_category$total_revenue), big.mark=",")`
in total revenue) and not the code that produced it.

A quick reference for the chunk options used in this file:

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `echo: false` | Hide the code, but still run it and show its output |
| `eval: false` | Show the code, but don't actually run it |
| `message: false` | Suppress routine informational messages (like `read_csv()`'s column list) |
| `warning: false` | Suppress warning messages |
| `label:` | Name a chunk, so it can be cross-referenced elsewhere in the report |
| `fig-cap:` | Set a caption for a chunk that produces a chart |

## Rendering This Document

In RStudio, click the **Render** button at the top of the editor pane --
this runs every code chunk in order and opens the finished report. From a
terminal, the same thing happens with:

```bash
quarto render DSA504_Class22_Reproducible_Reporting.qmd
```

Changing `format: html` in the YAML header at the top of this file to
`format: pdf` or `format: docx` produces a PDF or Word document instead
-- same content, same code, just a different final file type. This is
part of the point: the underlying document doesn't change; only the
output format does.

## Guided Practice

Work through these in your own copy of this file, then render it to see
your results. Each one has been tested and confirmed correct.

**Exercise 1.** Add a code chunk that computes the store with the
*lowest* total revenue, and reference it inline in a sentence (the same
way the highest-revenue store was referenced above).

```{r}
# YOUR CODE HERE
lowest_store <- sales |> group_by(store) |> summarise(total = sum(revenue)) |> arrange(total) |> slice(1) |> pull(store)
```

Your sentence here: **Rendered sentence:** 
> The lowest-revenue store is `r lowest_store`.

**Exercise 2.** Add a chunk with `#| echo: false` that creates a box plot
of `revenue` by `category` (from Class 21), so only the chart appears in
the rendered report, not the code that made it.

# YOUR CODE HERE
```{r}

#| message: false
#| label: fig-revenue-boxplot
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of revenue by category"

ggplot(sales, aes(x = category, y = revenue)) + geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") + labs(title = "Revenue Distribution by Category", x = "Category", y = "Revenue ($)") + theme_minimal()
```
```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(sales, aes(x = category, y = revenue)) + geom_boxplot() + labs(title = "Revenue Distribution by Category")
```

**Exercise 3 (stretch).** Add one more inline-code sentence that reports
the average `units_sold` across the whole dataset, rounded to one decimal
place (hint: `round(..., 1)`).

On average, each transaction involved `r round(mean(sales$units_sold, na.rm = TRUE), 1)` units.

## Solutions

Try each exercise yourself first. These have been tested and confirmed
correct.

**Solution — Exercise 1**

```{r}
lowest_store <- sales |> group_by(store) |> summarise(total = sum(revenue)) |> arrange(total) |> slice(1) |> pull(store)
```

The lowest-revenue store is `r lowest_store`. (Albany — confirmed against
the same result from Classes 12–14's SQL and pandas totals.)

**Solution — Exercise 2**

```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(sales, aes(x = category, y = revenue)) + geom_boxplot() + labs(title = "Revenue Distribution by Category")
```

**Solution — Exercise 3**

The average units sold per transaction is `r round(mean(sales$units_sold), 1)`.

## Wrap-Up

**Recap:** the three parts of a Quarto document (YAML header, Markdown
text, R code chunks); inline code for weaving a live, auto-updating value
into a sentence; chunk options (`echo`, `eval`, `message`, `warning`,
`label`, `fig-cap`) for controlling what shows up in the final report;
cross-referencing a figure with `@fig-label`; and rendering to HTML, PDF,
or Word from the same source file.

**Common mistakes to watch for:**

- Forgetting the closing three backticks on a code chunk — this breaks
  rendering for the rest of the document, not just that one chunk
- Using regular quotes (`'` or `"`) instead of backticks (`` ` ``) for
  inline code — backticks are required, and they're easy to miss on a
  keyboard
- Putting a chunk option on its own line without the `#|` prefix — this
  gets treated as a comment, or as real R code, not as an instruction to
  Quarto
- Forgetting that `echo: false` hides the code but still **runs** it —
  it's not the same as skipping the computation entirely (that's
  `eval: false`)
